induksjon (“induction”) + komfyr (“stove, cooker”), with linking -s- (“interfix”), literally “induction stove”. First attested before 2006
The first element induksjon (“induction”) is from Latin inductiō (“induction, introduction”), a verbal noun of indūcō (“to lead in, introduce”), from in- (“in, into”) + dūcō (“to lead, draw”), the latter ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to pull, draw; lead”). The second element komfyr (“stove, cooker”) ultimately belongs to the word family of Latin caleō (“to be warm”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱleh₁- (“hot, warm”).

8908.etyen: Compound of c (“C (the letter or musical note)”) + nøkkel (“key; clef; wrench”), literally “C key”. In the musical sense, the first component identifies the note indicated by the clef; in the tool sense, it refers to the curved shape of the head. The letter goes back to Latin C, from Etruscan 𐌂 (c), from Ancient Greek Γ (G, “gamma”), from Phoenician 𐤂 (g, “gimel”). The second component continues Middle Norwegian nykill, from Old Norse lykill (“key”), from Proto-Germanic *lukilaz, derived from *lūkaną (“to close, shut”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewg- (“to bend, turn”). The musical  / Compound of C (“C (a type designation)”) + nøkkel (“key”), literally “C key”. The first component designates a programming-key type in an electronic locking system. 1000140.etyen:
Borrowed from English Georgia (“U.S. state”). The English name was given in 1732 to the new British colony established by royal charter, in honour of George II of Great Britain. It is a Latinate feminine formation from the personal name George. The personal name is from Middle English George, from Old French Georges, from Latin Georgius, from Ancient Greek Γεώργιος (Geṓrgios, “George; literally “farmer””), from Ancient Greek γεωργός (geōrgós, “farmer, husbandman”), ultimately from γῆ (gê, “earth”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”).
Parallel borrowings and adaptations include Danish Georgia, Dutch Georgi
